questions.question: Explain why the six stages of the accounting cycle must happen in their fixed order — use the relationship between the journals and the ledger as your example.
questions.expected_answer: Every stage depends on the output of the stage before it. The ledger is posted from journal column totals, so the journals must be written up and totalled first; without journal totals there is nothing to post, and without posted ledger balances there is nothing to list in the trial balance.

questions.question: A classmate says: 'My trial balance agrees, so every entry in my books must be correct.' Correct their understanding.
questions.expected_answer: An agreeing trial balance only proves that total debits equal total credits — arithmetic equality. Errors like posting the correct amount to the wrong account on the correct side, omitting a transaction entirely, or entering a transaction twice leave the columns equal, so the books can still contain mistakes.

questions.question: Describe what each of the six stages produces, using one R240 cash sale at Khumalo Stores as your running example.
questions.expected_answer: The source document, the till slip, produces evidence of the sale; the Cash Receipts Journal produces a classified chronological record; posting produces updated balances in Bank and Sales; the trial balance produces a checked list of balances; the final accounts produce the gross and net profit; the financial statements produce the reports the owner reads.
